items.headline: Why perks for officials who quit to avoid inquiry: plea
items.gist: The Supreme Court issued notice to the Centre on a writ petition by Pratik Vora seeking a direction that constitutional functionaries, including judges, who resign rather than face transparent misconduct inquiries should be denied retirement perks and benefits they would have received had they completed tenure. The petition gains significance after Allahabad High Court judge Yashwant Varma’s resignation amid controversy over alleged misconduct.

items.headline: Govt. dropped use of OBC lists for Census as those featured ‘classes, not castes’, say officials
items.gist: Officials told The Hindu the government considered using Central and State Other Backward Classes lists for the 2027 Census but finalised an open-column caste enumeration method after concluding OBC lists describe classes rather than castes, with entries such as occupational groups or “local borns” that would not qualify as castes. Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes will be enumerated using Presidential lists as before, while Opposition leaders including Rahul Gandhi and Mallikarjun Kharge have demanded explicit OBC listing rather than an open column similar to problematic caste-name proliferation in the 2011 Socio-Economic Caste Census.

items.headline: Congress questions GDP revision, asks government to explain methodology
items.gist: The Congress on Thursday posed four questions over cumulative downward revisions of ₹43 lakh crore in estimated GDP size over four years, asking why estimates since 2022-23 were revised down, what drove the new methodology, who was consulted, and why the deflator appeared to understate inflation. Jairam Ramesh cited former Finance Secretary Subhash Chandra Garg’s calculation that nominal growth in the latest quarter would have been closer to 2.6% instead of 10.3% had earlier bases not been revised, and pointed to concerns raised by Arvind Subramanian and the IMF.

items.headline: Cong. leaders discuss issues in Punjab unit
items.gist: Congress top leadership including Rahul Gandhi and K.C. Venugopal met at Mallikarjun Kharge’s residence to discuss the leadership tussle in the Punjab unit ahead of Gandhi’s proposed yatra and elections early next year, though no official details were released.
items.paragraph: Congress top leadership including Rahul Gandhi and K.C. Venugopal met at Mallikarjun Kharge’s residence to discuss the leadership tussle in the Punjab unit ahead of Gandhi’s proposed yatra and elections early next year, though no official details were released. Former Chief Minister Charanjit Singh Channi and supporters had expressed displeasure over Scheduled Caste representation after not being made PCC chief or CM face; sources indicated the party may urge him to spearhead the poll campaign. In a separate meeting, leaders also discussed a possible Cabinet reshuffle in Himachal Pradesh with CM Sukhvinder Singh Sukhu.

items.headline: Cong. insulted Ram Temple, Army, says BJP leader
items.gist: BJP MP Sudhanshu Trivedi accused the Congress of an “anti-Army” and “anti-Shri Ram Temple” mindset at a press briefing, citing Rashid Alvi’s questions on the appointment of Air Marshal Jeetendra Mishra (retd) as CEO of the Shri Ram Janmabhoomi Teerth Kshetra Trust. Trivedi said Congress leaders had demanded proof of surgical and Balakot strikes and called the Army chief a “sadakchhap gunda,” and alleged that anyone still doubting Pakistan’s leaders after statements on Operation Sindoor harboured a “dimagi Naxal” mindset.

items.headline: IAF pilot who shot down Pak. plane joins regional airline
items.gist: Former IAF Group Captain and Vir Chakra awardee Abhinandan Varthaman has joined Goa-based regional airline FLY91 as a pilot, sources said. Varthaman, who downed an enemy jet in 2019 aerial combat with Pakistan and was held captive for three days, received the Vir Chakra in 2021 for “exceptional sense of duty”; FLY91, which began flying in March 2024 with six ATR 72-600 aircraft from Goa and Hyderabad bases, said he joined in August.

items.headline: Report warns against attempts to privatise ESIC
items.gist: ESI Ki Baat, a report on the Employees’ State Insurance Corporation prepared by Safe In India, warned the Union government against reported attempts to privatise ESIC and recommended raising the wage ceiling for coverage to ₹33,000 from ₹21,000. Releasing the report, ESIC Director General Ashok Kumar Singh said implementation of the Code on Social Security would help more workers avail ESIC benefits.

items.headline: Manipur polls may be hit if Naga-Kuki violence continues, says Deputy CM
items.gist: Manipur Deputy Chief Minister Losii Dikho said continuing Naga-Kuki violence in hill districts could make Assembly elections next year difficult and that Naga legislators may reconsider BJP support if concerns including removal of fellow Deputy CM Nemcha Kipgen are not addressed. The NPF leader told The Hindu that at least seven people were killed in Kangpokpi over the past week, Central forces had failed to prevent attacks on Naga villages, and Naga MLAs were prepared to take “extreme steps” if the Centre did not act on their memorandum to Amit Shah seeking Kipgen’s removal.

items.headline: States, Union Territories told to monitor glacial lakes
items.gist: Union Home Secretary Govind Mohan chaired a meeting with Himalayan States and Union Territories on Thursday to review preparedness for Glacial Lake Outburst Floods and snow avalanches, stressing proactive monitoring, risk-informed planning and stronger early warning systems in the aftermath of Nepal flash floods. He called for continuous surveillance of vulnerable glacial lakes and avalanche-prone regions and close coordination among State agencies, district administrations and scientific institutions to ensure timely action on warnings.

items.headline: Quality elementary teachers are vital to lives of children, nation-building: top court
items.gist: The Supreme Court emphasised educating elementary school teachers, saying children’s development and the nation’s future depend on their training, ahead of Teachers’ Day on September 5. Justice P.S.
items.paragraph: The Supreme Court emphasised educating elementary school teachers, saying children’s development and the nation’s future depend on their training, ahead of Teachers’ Day on September 5. items.headline: NRI deposits lift rupee to a two-month high of ₹94.6
items.gist: The Indian rupee appreciated to a two-month high of ₹94.60 against the dollar on September 3, a day after the RBI mopped up $137 billion through FCNR(B) deposits, external commercial borrowings and overseas foreign currency borrowings. The domestic currency opened at ₹94.30, down 50 paise from the previous close of ₹94.70, then gradually weakened to settle at the day’s closing level.

items.headline: SC disposes of SEBI appeals against NSE in two cases
items.gist: The Supreme Court disposed of SEBI appeals against NSE in co-location and dark fibre cases after a nearly ₹1,500 crore settlement, taking note of about ₹1,492 crore accepted in July—₹1,224 crore for co-location and ₹268 crore for dark fibre. The cases stem from allegations that brokers received preferential access to NSE trading systems via co-location following a 2015 whistle-blower complaint, and the resolution comes as NSE prepares an IPO expected to raise around ₹30,000 crore.

items.headline: Parliamentary panel flags 'punitive' tax regime, seeks data on new I-T Act's impact
items.gist: The Parliamentary Standing Committee on Finance, headed by BJP MP Bhartruhari Mahtab, criticised the Income Tax regime for relying excessively on “punitive action” and granting officials scope for overreach at a meeting on direct tax reforms with Revenue Department and CBDT representatives. Members flagged compliance glitches in the Income Tax Act, 2026, sought data on revenue collections, assessees and pending litigation, and expressed concern over individual taxpayers’ growing share relative to corporate collections and heavy-handed enforcement including retrospective rule changes.

items.headline: 'Little investment in energy innovation'
items.gist: IOCL chairman A. S.
items.paragraph: IOCL chairman A. S. Sahney lamented that barely 2% of India’s startup funding over the last 5–6 years—₹11,000 crore of about ₹5.5 lakh crore—went to energy, and excluding solar and wind it fell below ₹1,000 crore, at an MC2 Foundation event at CSIR-NCL in Pune. He said India’s energy demand will double in 15–20 years and the sector needs far more innovation and startups to match its importance as an energy nation.

items.headline: No excuses left for textiles sector, says Goyal on tariffs
items.gist: Commerce Minister Piyush Goyal said India’s textile industry can no longer blame external factors, noting developed markets now impose tariffs on Indian textile imports at par with or lower than those on Bangladesh and Vietnam after LDC advantages and Vietnam’s trade deals had long put India at a disadvantage. Goyal told a workshop that rates will be better or the same as competitors in almost all developed markets and “the ball is now entirely in our court” except for performance.

items.headline: Filatex's new unit to recycle polyester textiles
items.gist: Filatex India is investing about ₹300 crore to set up a polyester textile recycling plant in Gujarat with annual capacity of 27,000 tonne, expected to be commissioned next month. CMD Madhu Sudhan Bhageria said the plant will recycle polyester textile waste into polyester chips using in-house technology capable of recovering around 80–85% of polyester content from textile waste.

items.headline: GJC calls for balancing economic patriotism with cultural heritage
items.gist: The All India Gem & Jewellery Domestic Council welcomed Prime Minister Modi’s call to prioritise locally made products and reduce gold imports but said India must balance “economic patriotism” and cultural traditions, arguing the sector contributes nearly 7–8% to the economy and supports millions of livelihoods. The GJC was reacting to Modi’s repeated appeals to stop foreign trips and weddings, buy local, and purchase gold only if necessary.

items.headline: More than 40 crore Indians are caught in a healthcare gap: panel
items.gist: A Parliamentary Standing Committee on Health and Family Welfare report presented to Parliament last month says more than 40 crore Indians — over a quarter of the population — are too well off for government subsidies but not secure enough to absorb rising private healthcare costs, with over 60% of inpatient and 70% of outpatient care delivered privately. The panel made 368 recommendations and linked the "missing middle" vulnerability to low public health spending at 1.43% of GDP against the National Health Policy 2017 target of 2.5%, noting average private childbirth costs of ₹37,630 versus ₹2,299 in public facilities.

items.headline: Number of villages inundated by floods in north Odisha

items.headline: Jaishankar: India ready to extend 'any help' to end Ukraine war
items.gist: External Affairs Minister Dr S Jaishankar said India has consistently maintained that this is not an era of war and that solutions will not emerge from the battlefield, after meeting Ukrainian counterpart Andrii Sybiha in Kyiv. He reiterated Prime Minister Narendra Modi's statement from Bishkek two days earlier that endless war must give way to the end of war, and expressed India's support in any manner possible to end Ukraine's conflict with Russia.

items.headline: Viral Shaligram claim has no link to Nepal floods
items.gist: Videos circulating on social media claim that Nepal’s devastating August 26 flash floods unearthed the world’s largest Shaligram in Muktinath, supposedly over 170 million years old and weighing 30 tonnes, a claim amplified by Zee News and several social media users. A fact-check by Alt News found it misleading: Himalaya Times and Online Khabar reports from June 30, 2026, showed the same 22-foot-tall Shaligram sculpture in Mustang district was carved by artistes from the Nepal Academy of Fine Arts from a large rock on the Kali Gandaki’s banks in Jomsom between April 20 and May 4 and unveiled on May 28, with geolocation confirming it stands opposite Thakkhola Lodge & Jimihendrix Restaurant in Jomsom.

items.headline: Iran targets Kuwait in retaliation for US bombardments
items.gist: Iran fired at Kuwait on Thursday as part of its retaliation for US bombardments earlier in the week, with Kuwait's Ministry of Defence saying sirens sounded and air defences intercepted missiles and drones during "blatant Iranian aggression." The escalation followed US strikes on Iranian rocket launchers on an island in the Strait of Hormuz on Sunday, while Israeli police separately arrested a settler suspected in a West Bank attack on Palestinians and mourners buried two Palestinians aged 16 and 19 killed by Israeli forces in Al-Mughayyir.

items.headline: Rubio says no India-Iran trade deal
items.gist: US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said he did not think India and Iran were talking of a trade deal, telling The Brian Kilmeade Show on Fox News Radio that countries develop their own foreign policy and many nations around the world talk to the Iranian regime. His remarks came in response to Prime Minister Narendra Modi's meeting with Iranian President Massoud Pezeshkian on the sidelines of the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation Summit, and Rubio said President Donald Trump has made clear that no country should help Iran evade sanctions.

items.headline: Russia to shutter German cultural centres in tit-for-tat
items.gist: Russia will shutter German cultural centres across the country in a tit-for-tat measure, Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov said Thursday, after Berlin blamed Moscow for an attempted attack at Leipzig/Halle Airport and announced it was closing the Russian Consulate in Bonn and the Russian House cultural centre in Berlin. The move reflects soured relations and deepening tensions between Moscow and European countries helping Ukraine resist Russia's invasion amid repeated Western accusations of Russian sabotage campaigns.

items.headline: Chinese official warns of more glacier collapses
items.gist: A senior Chinese climate official warned that glaciers on the Tibetan Plateau are likely to become more unstable, potentially leading to more collapses and disasters similar to the August 26 ice-rock avalanche near the Nepal-Tibet border that devastated towns and villages in northern and central Nepal and killed hundreds. Gao Rong, deputy director of China's National Climate Centre, said glacier area on the plateau has shrunk by around 24 per cent over the past 60 years, with around 7,000 small glaciers disappearing completely.

items.headline: PM calls on B'deshis to protect existing harmony
items.gist: Prime Minister Tarique Rahman called on Bangladeshis to remain vigilant against anti-social forces trying to destroy the "existing atmosphere of harmony" in the country, speaking at a state-sponsored Janmashtami reception and honorarium programme for prominent Hindu community members, priests and temple custodians at Osmani Memorial Auditorium in Dhaka. Rahman said people of different faiths have lived together in Bangladesh for generations, maintaining mutual respect and harmony.

items.headline: South Asian American lawmakers seek concrete steps to fight hate
items.gist: A group of South Asian American elected representatives called for concrete steps to combat hate and prevent violence at a roundtable of officials of South Asian origin convened by Indian American Impact and Stop AAPI Hate at the US Capitol on Wednesday. US Congresspersons Raja Krishnamoorthi, Shri Thanedar, Ami Bera, Suhas Subramanyam and Pramila Jayapal attended, discussing strategies to strengthen prevention, reporting and response, including Krishnamoorthi's work on the Hate Crimes Commission Act.

items.headline: 2 dead, suspect killed in downtown Minneapolis
items.gist: Two people were killed and the suspect is dead after a shooting in a downtown Minneapolis apartment building on Wednesday afternoon, police said. items.headline: Putin cites chance of peace deal with Ukraine
items.gist: Russian President Vladimir Putin said on Thursday there was a chance of reaching an agreement to end the war in Ukraine, while Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said he expected a "new dynamic" in peace efforts. Speaking at an economic forum in Vladivostok, Putin said Russia and Ukraine must ultimately resolve the conflict, and in Kyiv Indian Foreign Minister S Jaishankar offered India's help in any manner if useful, recalling Prime Minister Narendra Modi's call in Bishkek for endless war to give way to the end of war.

items.headline: El Nino could be strongest in decades, warns UN
items.gist: The World Meteorological Organization warned on Thursday that El Nino is forecast to be the strongest since comparable records began four decades ago and is near certain to persist through February 2027. WMO chief Celeste Saulo said if the trajectory continues it may be stronger than anything since monitoring began, with the phenomenon set to peak towards the end of this year and knock-on climate impacts continuing well into 2027.

items.headline: Meloni's govt sets Italian longevity record
items.gist: Meloni's conservative administration became Italy's longest-serving uninterrupted government since World War II at 1,413 days on Thursday, surpassing the record set by the late Silvio Berlusconi between 2001 and 2005. Meloni and her party planned to celebrate the feat on Friday in Bari.

items.headline: Nepal flood death toll reaches 1,259
items.gist: Devastating floods on the China-Nepal border have killed at least 1,259 people in Nepal with 5,083 missing, while Chinese state media reported 21 killed in Tibet and 541 missing, taking the total toll from the August 26 disaster to 1,280 dead and 5,624 missing. Indian Ambassador Naveen Srivastava visited Syabrubesi and said Indian and Nepali teams have explored 100 metres inside the Chilime Power House tunnel using special equipment and will continue rescue work undeterred despite difficult terrain.

items.headline: Feminist icon Gloria Steinem dies at 92
items.gist: Gloria Steinem, the celebrated author and activist who became one of the most visible symbols and potent voices of the US women's movement and a co-founder of Ms Magazine, died on Wednesday at her home in New York City at 92. Much of her life as an advocate was spent on the road speaking at college campuses, community centres, rallies and marches, and she credited a 1969 speak-out on abortion rights with changing her career path after beginning as a journalist.

items.headline: Judge blocks Trump's new bid to curb birthright citizenship
items.gist: US District Judge Deborah L Boardman in Maryland granted a preliminary injunction blocking President Donald Trump's latest executive order targeting "birth tourism" until a class-action lawsuit brought by immigrant families and advocacy groups is resolved. Boardman wrote that "The Supreme Court has spoken: Children in the certified class are citizens at birth," noting birthright citizenship is guaranteed under current law for anyone born on US soil, with a few exceptions.

items.headline: Riots spread to Cape Town; march by ‘coloureds’ (FROM THE ARCHIVES 1976)
items.gist: Cape Town was rocked for a second day on September 3, 1976 by racial disturbances after about 3,000 coloured youths erupted in violence in the white centre, with unconfirmed reports that 5,000 coloured youths were marching from outlying black townships. Police opened fire at Trafalgar High School and with shotguns at demonstrators in the city centre, killing one person and wounding at least two others, while four people had been killed in disturbances in the city the previous day.

items.headline: 'Supersized' El Nino to be strongest ever recorded: UN
items.gist: The World Meteorological Organisation said on Thursday that El Nino is set to intensify into 2027 and could be the strongest ever recorded, with near 100% likelihood of persistence through February 2027 fuelled by exceptionally warm Pacific Ocean temperatures—the first time WMO has expressed such certainty. Secretary-General Celeste Saulo said if the trajectory continues it may be stronger than anything since monitoring began, potentially shifting global rainfall and temperature patterns and fuelling droughts and typhoons as WMO steps up preparedness efforts.

items.headline: The feminist organiser and her everyday rebellions
items.gist: Gloria Steinem (1934–2026), described on her website as a “feminist organizer,” is remembered for movement-building through Talking Circles at her New York home and decades of activism including founding Ms. magazine and chairing Apne Aap Women Worldwide’s advisory board.
items.paragraph: Gloria Steinem (1934–2026), described on her website as a “feminist organizer,” is remembered for movement-building through Talking Circles at her New York home and decades of activism including founding Ms. magazine and chairing Apne Aap Women Worldwide’s advisory board. Steinem, who spent two years in India after graduating Smith College in 1956 and co-edited As if Women Matter with Ruchira Gupta, wrote nine books, reframed abortion as “reproductive freedom,” and influenced feminist thought globally; colleagues recall her India ties, her Kali cover on Ms.’s first issue selling 3 lakh copies, and her humour and accessibility until her death.

items.headline: Foreign arms, drones fuel Sudan war, says UN probe
items.gist: A UN fact-finding mission said on Thursday that foreign weapons, military technology, fighters and logistical networks are sustaining Sudan’s conflict and expanding warring parties’ ability to strike distant civilian areas with drones. Investigators found grounds to believe a network involving individuals and entities in the UAE, Chad, Libya and Somalia supplied the RSF with weapons, equipment, logistics, training and foreign personnel, while external support for Sudan’s military was at an early stage.

items.headline: Excess deaths during heatwaves in Belgium between June-August
items.gist: Belgium recorded 2,935 excess deaths during successive heatwaves between June and August 2026, according to the Sciensano national public health institute, with 2,035 extra deaths between June 18 and July 3 and another 535 between July 4 and 17.

items.headline: Alcaraz shrugs off early setback to forge ahead
items.gist: Defending U.S. Open champion Carlos Alcaraz rebounded from dropping the first set to beat Jaime Faria 4-6, 6-0, 6-3, 6-2 on Wednesday night in New York, winning eight straight games after a mid-first-set break.
items.paragraph: Defending U.S. Open champion Carlos Alcaraz rebounded from dropping the first set to beat Jaime Faria 4-6, 6-0, 6-3, 6-2 on Wednesday night in New York, winning eight straight games after a mid-first-set break. The No. 2 seed, returning from a four-month right wrist injury that sidelined him from the French Open and Wimbledon, said four sets helped test his body and that he is no longer in pain. Alcaraz is on a 16-match Grand Slam winning streak with seven major titles and did not drop a set until last year's final against Jannik Sinner; Daniil Medvedev called him a top title favourite despite uncertainty over how his wrist will hold up.

items.headline: Aryna powers her way into 3rd round of US Open in just 53 min
items.gist: Top-seeded Aryna Sabalenka beat Polina Iatcenko 6-1, 6-1 in 53 minutes on Wednesday to reach the U.S. Open third round, looking ready to pursue a third straight Flushing Meadows title after recent fourth-round exits.
items.paragraph: Top-seeded Aryna Sabalenka beat Polina Iatcenko 6-1, 6-1 in 53 minutes on Wednesday to reach the U.S. Open third round, looking ready to pursue a third straight Flushing Meadows title after recent fourth-round exits. Rain suspended play on outside courts while matches under Arthur Ashe and Louis Armstrong roofs continued; Jessica Pegula beat Sofia Kenin 6-3, 6-1 in 56 minutes, No. 8 Ben Shelton defeated Hubert Hurkacz 6-3, 5-7, 7-6 (3), 7-5, and No. 7 Daniil Medvedev beat Sebastian Gorzny 6-3, 6-3, 7-5 after a brief delay when two birds sat on the net. Sabalenka won 15 of 16 first-serve points in the opening set and went 21 for 28 on first serve in the match.

items.headline: Naqvi hits back at Pak cricket critics
items.gist: PCB Chairman Mohsin Naqvi, speaking in London, lashed out at criticism of Pakistan's Test team after 0-2 losses to England, saying detractors "have never achieved anything in their lives." He cited other teams' losses to weaker opponents, including India's recent T20 defeats to Ireland, to argue setbacks do not define a side. Naqvi and the PCB faced fire after replacing seven players in the England tour squad with mostly young names in the three-match series.

items.headline: BCCI leaves Rohit's future up in the air
items.gist: The BCCI performance review meeting on Thursday did little to clarify Rohit Sharma’s ODI future, with secretary Devajit Saikia brushing aside speculation by citing Rohit’s 138 in the July 19 Lord’s ODI against England and stressing it was not a selection meeting focused instead on England, Ireland and the 2027 World Cup roadmap. The Hindu understands the selection committee had told Rohit during the June Chennai ODI against Afghanistan he was not in plans beyond the England series, but BCCI administrators overruled that before Lord’s; with chief selector Ajit Agarkar absent, the question was deliberately left unresolved.

items.headline: Asian Games: Yashvir comes in for Neeraj
items.gist: Commonwealth Games bronze medallist javelin thrower Yashvir Singh has been named Neeraj Chopra's replacement in the men's javelin for the upcoming Asian Games as per the latest 77-member Asiad team released by the Athletics Federation of India. Neeraj prematurely ended his season due to an ankle ligament tear after securing silver at the Glasgow Commonwealth Games and recording 88.05m at the Lausanne Diamond League, and Abhishek Pal's name is missing from the list after the distance runner reportedly tested positive for a banned substance.

items.headline: Alcaraz and Sabalenka advance to the third round with ease
items.gist: Defending champions Carlos Alcaraz and Aryna Sabalenka advanced at the US Open on Wednesday as organisers cleared a rain-delayed backlog, with Alcaraz dropping the opening set before beating Jaime Faria 4-6, 6-0, 6-3, 6-2 and Sabalenka crushing Polina Iatcenko 6-1, 6-1. Former winner Daniil Medvedev, Iga Swiatek, Naomi Osaka, Linda Noskova, Jessica Pegula, Ben Shelton and Frances Tiafoe also progressed, with Medvedev overcoming an avian interruption during a 6-1, 6-3, 7-5 win over Sebastian Gorzny.

items.headline: Alcaraz plans to play fewer events
items.gist: Carlos Alcaraz said Wednesday he plans to play fewer tournaments in future, blaming an "impossible" tennis calendar for a rising number of injuries, and that he would take breaks of one or two months and miss some tournaments because it is impossible to play them all.

items.headline: BCCI to prioritise rest, practice matches, acclimatisation before series in SENA nations
items.gist: BCCI secretary Devajit Saikia said after a review meeting that the board will work to ensure proper rest, acclimatisation and practice matches before major series in SENA countries, citing too many matches in a year as a challenge for the next Future Tours Programme. The meeting attended by Shubman Gill, Shreyas Iyer, Gautam Gambhir and VVS Laxman also reviewed India's poor England and Ireland tours and mapped plans for the 2027 ODI World Cup.

items.headline: Smriti scales the summit as India enters semifinals
items.gist: Smriti Mandhana’s 64-ball 124 (14 fours, seven sixes) powered India to 193 for five and a 137-run win over Hong Kong in Dubai, sealing a Women’s Asia Cup semifinal berth as Hong Kong were bowled out for 56. Smriti surpassed Mithali Raj’s 10,868 runs to become the leading run-getter in women’s internationals with 10,880, went past Meg Lanning and Laura Wolvaardt for most hundreds (18) across formats, and became the first Indian woman with two T20I centuries; India next face Pakistan on September 5.

items.headline: MULETHI for hair growth
items.gist: Mulethi (Glycyrrhiza glabra), or licorice root, is an Ayurvedic botanical rich in glycyrrhizin, flavonoids, and phytoestrogens that soothes inflamed scalps, combats Malassezia yeast behind dandruff, improves microcirculation to follicles, and inhibits 5-alpha-reductase to reduce DHT-linked hair thinning, while its mucilage helps retain moisture and reduce breakage. Home remedies include a weekly mulethi–curd–honey mask (2 tablespoons mulethi powder, 3–4 tablespoons curd, 1 teaspoon honey, left on 30–45 minutes), a mulethi-infused coconut or sesame oil scalp massage 1–2 times weekly, and a mulethi–amla scalp spray boiled in water and applied after washing without rinsing.

items.headline: Understanding pineapple, bromelain and cancer
items.gist: Pineapple (Ananas comosus) is rich in vitamin C, manganese, dietary fiber, and antioxidants, and contains bromelain—proteolytic enzymes concentrated mainly in the stem and juice that laboratory research has studied for anti-inflammatory and antitumor effects. Purified bromelain extracts in cell and animal studies can induce apoptosis in breast, colon, and melanoma cell lines, inhibit metastasis, reduce inflammatory pathways such as NF-κB and COX-2, and degrade extracellular matrix around solid tumors, but eating whole pineapple yields far lower enzyme doses, bromelain is partially broken down in digestion, and robust human trials proving cancer prevention or treatment are lacking.
items.paragraph: Pineapple (Ananas comosus) is rich in vitamin C, manganese, dietary fiber, and antioxidants, and contains bromelain—proteolytic enzymes concentrated mainly in the stem and juice that laboratory research has studied for anti-inflammatory and antitumor effects. Pineapple or bromelain supplements must not replace chemotherapy, radiation, or surgery; bromelain can act as a mild blood thinner and interact with anticoagulants such as warfarin, and people allergic to latex, pollen, or papain may react to pineapple or concentrated bromelain.

items.headline: Understanding systemic lupus erythematosus
items.gist: Systemic Lupus Erythematosus (SLE), commonly known as lupus, is a complex chronic autoimmune disorder in which the immune system loses tolerance and produces autoantibodies that target healthy tissues, causing variable flares and remission across organ systems. It is driven by genetic predisposition (over 100 linked loci, including HLA-DR2 and HLA-DR3), environmental triggers such as UV light, Epstein-Barr virus, certain drugs, and stress, and hormonal factors—roughly 90% of patients are women aged 15–44.
items.paragraph: Systemic Lupus Erythematosus (SLE), commonly known as lupus, is a complex chronic autoimmune disorder in which the immune system loses tolerance and produces autoantibodies that target healthy tissues, causing variable flares and remission across organ systems. It is driven by genetic predisposition (over 100 linked loci, including HLA-DR2 and HLA-DR3), environmental triggers such as UV light, Epstein-Barr virus, certain drugs, and stress, and hormonal factors—roughly 90% of patients are women aged 15–44. Symptoms range from profound fatigue, low-grade fever, and a malar “butterfly” rash to photosensitivity, discoid lesions, Raynaud’s phenomenon, and non-erosive arthritis in over 90% of patients; diagnosis relies on medical history, ACR/EULAR criteria, ANA testing (positive in over 95%), specific autoantibodies including Anti-dsDNA and Anti-Sm, and complement levels C3 and C4.

items.headline: Here's why the soil is BROWN
items.gist: Soil gets its rich brown colour from a blend of decomposed plant and animal matter (humus) and weathered minerals, primarily iron. When leaves, roots, and tiny organisms die, soil microbes digest them into humus, which is rich in carbon and gives topsoil a deep brown-to-black shade; oxidized iron from earth’s crust meeting oxygen and water creates yellow, red, and warm brown mineral tints.
items.paragraph: Soil gets its rich brown colour from a blend of decomposed plant and animal matter (humus) and weathered minerals, primarily iron. When leaves, roots, and tiny organisms die, soil microbes digest them into humus, which is rich in carbon and gives topsoil a deep brown-to-black shade; oxidized iron from earth’s crust meeting oxygen and water creates yellow, red, and warm brown mineral tints. Soil colour varies with local climate, drainage, and biological activity—dark brown or black indicates high humus and fertility, bright red or orange points to high iron oxides and low organic matter, yellow forms when iron hydrates, gray or blue-green occurs in waterlogged conditions, and white or pale soil signals salt, quartz sand, or leached nutrients.

items.headline: Lessons from a jam
items.gist: Traffic jams expose human impatience and can teach management lessons while waiting for traffic to move. Management consultant Vriddhi Chawla suggests finding the actual bottleneck before asking people to work faster, noting that a designer waiting for content, a content team waiting for approval, or an approver stuck in another meeting may be the real blocker; HR consultant Riddhima Baweja warns that adding more people to a struggling project can create chaos and pull pace down without clear directions; Chawla also stresses that people should know who is responsible for what and how communication hierarchy works; psychologist Vijaya notes patience when things do not move at the desired pace, and the takeaway is that good management requires clear communication, giving people space, avoiding unnecessary changes, and sometimes waiting strategically.

items.headline: What your routine says
items.gist: It is known that daily routine strongly reflects what matters to us and defines our priorities, making it important to have a routine that keeps you connected with the right priorities. Dr Prajakta Gupte, Consultant Psychiatry at Jupiter Hospital, Thane, says priorities are visible in where time, energy, and attention go—starting the day with exercise and balanced meals suggests health and self-discipline rank high, while a routine dominated by work, constant notifications, and little rest suggests productivity over well-being; business and life coach Sanjuri Ray calls daily routines an honest record of what really matters, warning that a day run by whoever messages first can quietly rewrite identity.

items.headline: Left on read?
items.gist: In the age of instant communication, even a few hours of silence can feel significant, and a delayed reply may trigger uncertainty, overthinking, or anxiety despite having little to do with the relationship itself. Clinical psychologist Elza Dsouza explains that without tone or facial expressions, silence can feel like rejection, and the key is to separate facts from interpretations; Gen Z content creator Snehal D’Souza describes hesitating to double-text for fear of seeming too eager or desperate when left on read; Mumbai counsellor Deepal Mehta says a delayed reply becomes a blank canvas for fears, where checking online status and rereading messages can reinforce anxiety, and that a delayed response is a fact while what we believe it means is an assumption.

items.headline: Know your English
items.gist: From the archives of November 13, 2001, S. Upendran explains that "bolt from the blue" or "bolt out of the blue" means something sudden and totally unexpected, that "vox populi" or "vox pop" is Latin for "voice of the people" and denotes street interviews used in broadcasting, that "plenty" and "aplenty" both mean large amounts but "aplenty" is old-fashioned and usually follows the noun, and that both "motherland" and "fatherland" are acceptable depending on language and culture.

items.headline: Inside the mind of Singeetham Srinivasa Rao: a masterclass in storytelling

Reddy — who taught him to write "dark cave" not just "cave" — and on contrast and musical narration for comedy and economy.

items.headline: ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude face outages; AWS also affected
items.gist: Major artificial intelligence platforms, including OpenAI’s ChatGPT, Google Gemini and Anthropic’s Claude, experienced significant service disruptions on Thursday, affecting thousands of users globally, according to outage tracking website Downdetector. The disruption also appeared to impact Grok and Amazon Web Services, with users reporting website inaccessibility and internal server errors.

items.headline: Indian envoys explore global partnerships in tech, investment, innovation in K'taka
items.gist: Indian envoys to the US and Azerbaijan visited Karnataka and held high-level meetings with the governor, chief minister and senior ministers, exploring opportunities to expand economic, technological, investment and institutional partnerships, the Consulate General of India in Los Angeles said. items.headline: Human Rights body seeks reports on Insta ads linked to child sex abuse
items.gist: The National Human Rights Commission has directed the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology, the Ministry of Information and Broadcasting and the Delhi Police to submit point-wise action-taken reports within two weeks in a case involving paid Instagram advertisements that allegedly facilitated access to child sexual abuse material. The NHRC bench led by Priyank Kanoongo took cognisance after BBC World Service reports alleged that paid advertisements using terms like 'rape video' and 'child video' bypassed Meta's review mechanisms and directed users to Telegram channels where the material was allegedly available for sale.

items.headline: Mamdani frowns on AI use for New York students; imposes 1-yr ban
items.gist: New York City public schools will temporarily bar elementary and middle school students from using generative artificial intelligence tools during the upcoming school year, Mayor Zohran Mamdani said on Wednesday, in what officials described as the most expansive such prohibition in the United States. The one-year moratorium bars student-facing generative AI software through eighth grade, affecting roughly 600,000 public school students, halts use of about 40 educational AI tools, and bans companion chatbots across all grade levels, while high schoolers are exempt from the full ban.

items.headline: Silicon Valley's big money is about to get a lot bigger
items.gist: As Anthropic and OpenAI prepare to go public, at least 95 investors have put money into both companies, according to PitchBook — a break from the old venture-capital norm of backing only one rival in a category. Anthropic has raised more than $130 billion from roughly 300 investors and OpenAI more than $180 billion from roughly 230, dwarfing Facebook's $2.4 billion and Uber's roughly $20 billion before their IPOs; Anthropic's listing could value it at $2 trillion.

items.headline: Govt plans social media code for employees
items.gist: Amid a growing trend of government staff posting reels, videos and personal opinions on platforms such as X, Facebook and Instagram, the Centre is working on a social media code of conduct for its officers and employees. The proposal has been deliberated at the highest levels of government and is expected to apply across ranks, though the timeline and specific provisions are not yet known.
items.paragraph: Amid a growing trend of government staff posting reels, videos and personal opinions on platforms such as X, Facebook and Instagram, the Centre is working on a social media code of conduct for its officers and employees. The proposal has been deliberated at the highest levels of government and is expected to apply across ranks, though the timeline and specific provisions are not yet known. The move comes amid broader efforts to tighten online content regulation, including reducing the time available to social media platforms to act on sensitive content from 24 hours to two hours under amendments to the Information Technology Rules, 2021, notified on February 10.

items.headline: When oil becomes a weapon, India must fuel its way (Opinion)
items.gist: The latest US-Iran confrontation underscores India's vulnerability to imported crude oil dependence, and ethanol-blended petrol is framed as an energy-security imperative beyond environmental policy. India achieved its 20% ethanol-blending target in 2025-26, up from less than 1.5% in 2013-14, with ethanol production capacity expanding nearly fivefold since 2014.

items.headline: Waiving tuition fee for SC, ST students (Opinion)
items.gist: The Odisha government’s decision to waive admission fees for Scheduled Caste and Scheduled Tribe students securing seats in State-run medical and engineering colleges addresses a financial barrier in higher education, the writer argues, but institutions should also extend subsidised accommodation, accessible study materials, and mentorship to ensure sustainable academic success. States across the country should emulate such targeted welfare measures while strengthening foundational schooling to level the playing field early.

items.headline: JCB to bouquet: Protest turns a youthful slip (Opinion)
items.gist: Richard Lloyd writes that after the government and Supreme Court softened toward protesters, FIRs once treated seriously became cases everyone wanted closed, with the government telling the court it had no objection to ending them and the court invoking Article 142 for “complete justice” without investigation or trial, chiefly to protect students’ futures. He asks whether constitutional compassion should depend on a student identity card when farmers, workers, and pensioners also protest, warns that justice must not appear more forgiving depending on who stands before it, and cautions against a model where the State registers an FIR, the government changes its mind, Article 142 is invoked, and everyone goes home happy.

items.headline: Growth rate is not the whole story (Opinion)
items.gist: India's economy grew 7.8% in the April-June quarter, ahead of RBI forecasts, while nominal GDP grew 10.3%, pointing to investment-led expansion as real gross fixed capital formation rose 11.9% against 7.1% for private final consumption. Deepanshu Mohan argues MoSPI's February GDP rebasing to 2022-23, with methodological changes including double deflation, has revised consumption's share down by about 9-11% over three years while lifting investment's measured share, meaning the headline rate does not tell the full story of who benefits; he calls for prosperity-driven rather than growth-obsessed policy, citing East Asian manufacturing-led models.

items.headline: Welcome move (Opinion)
items.gist: At the Union government’s request, the Supreme Court invoked Article 142 to quash criminal cases against youth who joined nationwide Gen Z protests led by the Cockroach Janta Party over examination reforms and government accountability, including demands to withdraw FIRs registered during the July agitations, while directing that no fresh FIRs be filed. The editorial contrasts this relief with the Centre’s handling of largely peaceful farmer protests and anti-CAA demonstrations, where serious charges including terrorism and sedition were invoked and many protesters remain jailed, and argues the Court should extend the same standard to those cases so the CJP relief does not remain an exception.

items.headline: Youth power, an electoral force still in the making (Opinion)
items.gist: Akshay Rout writes that while Gen Z street protests have forced parties to engage with youth issues, India’s largest youth cohort has not yet consolidated into a predictable electoral bloc, with no discernible youth voting trend in recent Assembly polls in Tamil Nadu, Assam, West Bengal, Keralam and Puducherry. About 65% of India’s population is below 35 and roughly 23% of the electorate is aged 18–29, but caste, community and gender identities have largely subsumed youth identity, and upcoming polls in Uttarakhand, Uttar Pradesh, Punjab, Manipur and Goa will test whether street noise translates into organised political preference.

items.headline: For newborns, the answer is hospital plus home (Opinion)
items.gist: Abhay Bang argues that rising institutional deliveries — from 39% in 2005–06 to 90% in 2023–24 — have overcrowded Special Newborn Care Units, contributing to clustered newborn deaths including three killed in an August 24, 2026 fire at Amravati’s government women’s hospital. Citing the Gadchiroli trial’s 62.2% neonatal mortality reduction through home-based neonatal care by trained ASHAs, he advocates a three-part strategy of decongesting units via strengthened home care, improving facility staffing and safety, and ensuring not every newborn who needs care requires a hospital bed.

items.headline: Exclusions cannot define electoral roll 'purification' (Opinion)
items.gist: Kamal Laddha of Bengaluru writes that 13 crore names omitted from draft electoral rolls in the first three phases of the SIR reveal a document-heavy EC process biased toward exclusions, and that West Bengal tribunal reinstatements suggest many absent-or-shifted omissions elsewhere may be incorrect; he argues the EC cannot claim purification success on exclusion counts alone unless it onboards every eligible citizen, especially vulnerable and marginalised voters, in the constitutional spirit of universal adult suffrage.

items.headline: Bengaluru's SIR puzzles (Opinion)
items.gist: Kepu Subrahmanya writes that Karnataka's draft SIR roll excluded 1.08 crore of 5.54 crore pre-SIR voters, with 75% in absent or shifted categories, and that in 13 of 28 Bengaluru Urban assembly seats enumerated voters fall below 2024 Lok Sabha votes polled—and in six seats below 2023 assembly votes—an anomaly CM D K Shivakumar wants more enumeration time to resolve. He notes rural constituencies broadly show realistic outcomes with over 85% enrolment in about 150 of 224 seats, while 51 urban seats including Bengaluru and major cities recorded SIR enrolment below the 80.52% state average, correlating with low 2023 turnout, whereas Mangaluru escaped the worst list though with relatively lower enrolment.

items.headline: Yet my name has been classified as 'shifted' (Opinion)
items.gist: Under SPEAK OUT, with an epigraph quoting Amelia Atwater-Rhodes — "Fate has a twisted sense of humour" — Rajya Sabha MP Raghav Chadha says he is a sitting MP from Punjab with voter ID registered in Mohali, yet his name has been classified as "shifted" in the draft electoral rolls.

items.headline: Resilience now for future droughts (Opinion)
items.gist: With Karnataka facing a 23% monsoon deficit against India's 14% rainfall gap and about 20 lakh hectares of an 84-lakh-hectare kharif target still unsown, including 15 lakh hectares of cereals, the editorial warns deficient rains, falling groundwater, and crop vulnerability have driven a record 37 lakh crop insurance applications. It urges short-term drinking-water priority in drought-hit rural and urban areas—including Bengaluru, which saw 63% August rainfall shortage and dry borewells—while calling for long-term watershed development, aquifer recharge, rainwater harvesting, crop shifts from water-intensive paddy and sugarcane, and strict Bengaluru enforcement of harvesting, wastewater recycling, and lake revival rather than treating drought as exceptional.

items.headline: Food safety: Message in large print (Opinion)
items.gist: The editorial welcomes FSSAI's Supreme Court-backed proposal for prominent red hexagonal front-of-pack warning labels on foods high in sugar, salt, fat and similar nutrients, arguing small back-of-pack print fails consumers while stage-wise FOPNL starting with warnings for products exceeding limits on two or more components is only a credible start. It urges separate clear markers for every nutrient of concern, strict time-bound implementation after years of delay and industry resistance, and public awareness campaigns, noting India faces rising diabetes, hypertension, obesity and cholesterol linked to unhealthy diets and that the apex court told FSSAI to prioritise citizens' health over multinational interests.

items.headline: Are brands overreacting to manufactured outrage? (Opinion)
items.gist: In a Parley conversation moderated by Sonikka Loganathan, communications leader Mitushi Sharma and Think9 founder Santosh Desai discuss Giva withdrawing a Raksha Bandhan advertisement after netizens criticised Kriti Sanon’s outfit as too revealing, following similar backlashes against Tanishq’s 2020 interfaith ad and Fab India’s 2021 Jashn-e-Riwaaz campaign. Sharma and Desai debate whether brands are reacting from fear, employee safety concerns or commercial caution, and whether such withdrawals reflect manufactured outrage and growing self-censorship rather than genuine cultural sensitivity.

items.headline: Jealousy is dependency in disguise (Opinion)
items.gist: Acharya Prashant writes that jealousy reveals where self-worth is kept — not in one's own work but in others' praise — and that hating someone praised feels like theft when one was only carrying "borrowed jewellery." He argues moralising or suppressing jealousy only poisons it, while a jealous ego needs others to remain lower and cannot truly admire excellence; building confidence merely upgrades the external supply rather than ending dependence.

items.headline: Keeping pace with a succession of climate shock events (Opinion)
items.gist: Meera Srinivasan writes that Nepal’s Rasuwa floods, with over 1,250 lives lost and more than 4,000 still missing, and Sri Lanka’s Cyclone Ditwah highlight unequal vulnerabilities across South Asia, including marginalised Malaiyaha Tamil estate workers in Sri Lanka who remain displaced months later. She notes repeated regional climate shocks from Pakistan’s 2022 floods to Nepal’s 2026 disaster, and cites former diplomat Shyam Saran’s 2009 argument that South Asia is an ecologically interconnected system needing collaborative climate response rather than isolated disaster coverage.

items.headline: Demolition needs a uniform policy (Opinion)
items.gist: Lakshita Handa writes that on August 12 a Supreme Court bench headed by the Chief Justice considered a petition for a uniform pan-India policy on demolition of unauthorised constructions, noting demolition must go hand in hand with rehabilitation. Citing a 2024 judgment barring punitive demolitions without due process, she points to Delhi's intensified crackdown — since June 1 the Municipal Corporation of Delhi has demolished 681 unauthorised properties and sealed 398 — and argues states should mandate at least 30 days' show-cause notice, personal hearings, restricted use of force, and three-to-six months' rehabilitation for those rendered homeless, especially vulnerable groups.

items.headline: Punjab: From breadbasket to a crisis of opportunity (Opinion)
items.gist: Lt Gen Bhopinder Singh (retd) writes that Punjab, once India's Green Revolution breadbasket, now faces depleted groundwater from water-intensive paddy, farm indebtedness, industrial stagnation, drug addiction, unemployment and youth leaving "in hoards" abroad because home offers too few possibilities. As the state braces for elections, he argues public discourse is dominated by religion, caste and intra-party power struggles rather than a credible long-term plan for agricultural reform, water conservation, industrial investment and making staying home a credible choice rather than an act of sacrifice.

items.headline: The charioteer of devotees (Opinion)
items.gist: In the FAITH column, Damal S Ramakrishnan writes that Krishna chose Vasudeva and Devaki as birth parents under Rohini on Ashtami in Avani to vanquish Kamsa, yet remained on earth to attain guru status and reinforce the acharya’s role. After vanquishing Kamsa, marrying Rukmini, protecting Draupadi and delivering the Bhagavad Gita as charioteer to mankind, Krishna studied under sage Sandipini, restored his guru’s son as dakshina, and at Kurukshetra became Gita acharya when Arjuna refused to fight relatives, combining karma, gnana and bhakti yoga in 15 chapters.

items.headline: Silken touch and a stunning range (Opinion)
items.gist: P.K. Ajith Kumar writes that Smriti Mandhana, who told The Hindu in Jaipur seven years ago that her mother instilled perseverance and that she wanted to be the world’s best batter, has made batting a fine art comparable to David Gower or Sourav Ganguly as records continue to flow.

During Thursday’s 124 against Hong Kong she passed Mithali Raj’s 10,868 international runs at age 30 with many years likely ahead, remaining driven to stay at the top of women’s cricket.

items.headline: The Pakistan-sized mess (Opinion)
items.gist: R. Kaushik writes that Pakistani cricket has become predictably messy, with the Pakistan Cricket Board's unprecedented mid-series move to banish seven players — including former captains Salman Ali Agha and Mohammad Rizwan — along with head coach Sarfaraz Ahmed and bowling coach Umar Gul after heavy defeats in England ranking among its most bizarre reactions.
points: R.

The piece argues that constant chopping and changing of selection panels, captains, players and coaching staff has left Pakistan at the bottom of the World Test Championship standings and that incoming coach Mike Hesson and Babar Azam must rebuild with faith and patience as Joe Root's England eye a 3-0 sweep from Birmingham.

items.headline: Why accessible rehabilitation is the need of the hour in India (Opinion)
items.gist: On World Physiotherapy Day, the authors cite Sidhartha Bandha's father's stroke to show how distant, costly physiotherapy left him with contractures after hospital care saved his life, and note that India has only about 52,000 practising physiotherapists — 0.36 per 10,000 people — with most concentrated in cities. They call for community-based learning, home rehabilitation support, tele-rehabilitation, and rural postings so physiotherapy is treated as lifesaving care rather than an optional add-on.

items.headline: The gap in manufacturing sector GVA (Opinion)
items.gist: Jatinder S. Bedi and R.
points: Jatinder S.
Bedi and R.

Nagaraj write that National Accounts Statistics puts manufacturing gross value added at ₹38.6 lakh crore for 2023-24 — 14.7% of GDP — but an alternative estimate from Annual Survey of Industries and Annual Survey of Unincorporated Sector Enterprises data totals ₹27.4 lakh crore, a 40.9% gap.

Even after adding an estimated ₹3.6 lakh crore from residual workers not captured in those surveys, the potential GVA of ₹31.0 lakh crore still falls 24.5% short of the official figure, leaving ₹7.6 lakh crore unexplained unless MCA-21 corporate data and NSO methodologies are opened for independent verification.
